did_you_know.text: Did you know? Abimelech was the son of Gideon, who is called Jerubbaal here. He first approached his maternal uncles and his mother’s family to gain support in Shechem.
Did you know? The leaders of Shechem funded Abimelech with seventy pieces of silver taken from the temple of Baal-berith. With this money, he hired worthless and reckless men to follow him.
Did you know? Abimelech killed Jerubbaal’s seventy sons on one stone, but Jotham, the youngest son, escaped because he hid himself.
Did you know? After Abimelech was made king, Jotham stood on Mount Gerizim and proclaimed his parable to the leaders of Shechem, asking them to listen to him.

Did you know? In the parable of the trees, the olive tree, the fig tree, and the vine refuse to become king because they do not want to stop producing their fruit and fulfilling their roles. Only the thornbush agrees to accept the kingship.
Did you know? The thornbush offers the trees shelter in its shade, but warns that if they do not accept its rule, fire will come out of it and consume even the cedars of Lebanon.
Did you know? Abimelech ruled over Israel for only three years. Afterward, hostility arose between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.

Did you know? When Gaal saw Abimelech’s men, Zebul tried to deceive him, claiming that he was seeing only the shadows of the mountains. When the army drew closer, Zebul mocked Gaal and urged him to go out and fight.
Did you know? After capturing Shechem, Abimelech killed its inhabitants, destroyed the city, and sowed it with salt—a symbolic act signifying its destruction.

Did you know? At Thebez, a woman dropped a millstone on Abimelech’s head and mortally wounded him. Abimelech asked his armor-bearer to kill him so that no one would say a woman had killed him. At the end of the chapter, his death and the destruction at Shechem are described as the retribution for the evil Abimelech and the people of Shechem had done.
